definition: A response field saying why Claude stopped, e.g. `end_turn` (finished naturally) or `max_tokens` (hit your limit).
whyItMatters: Your code must branch on it: use the reply on `end_turn`, run tools on `tool_use`, raise the limit or continue on `max_tokens`.
example: Others: `stop_sequence` (emitted one of your stop sequences), `tool_use` (calling a tool), `pause_turn`, `refusal`.

definition: The top-level Messages API field for instructions that apply from the start of a conversation, such as a goal or role.
whyItMatters: Put standing instructions in the top-level `system` field: a `system` message can't be the first entry in `messages`.
example: Some newer models (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5) also accept `"role": "system"` messages after a user turn.

definition: The maximum number of tokens to generate before stopping. The model may stop **before** reaching it; it is only an absolute ceiling on output.
whyItMatters: If a reply ends with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` it was truncated: raise the limit or continue the response.
example: `"max_tokens": 1024` caps the reply at 1,024 output tokens.

definition: Setting `"stream": true` on a Messages request returns the response incrementally as server-sent events (SSE).
whyItMatters: A UI can show text as it is generated, and the SDKs require streaming for large `max_tokens` values to avoid HTTP timeouts.
example: Events: `message_start`, `content_block_delta`s, `message_delta`, `message_stop`. Show each `text_delta` as it arrives.

definition: The measurable targets an LLM app must meet. Good criteria are **specific**, **measurable**, **achievable** and **relevant** to the app's purpose and users.
whyItMatters: An LLM app starts with clear criteria, then evals that measure them. Instead of "good performance", specify e.g. an F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out test set.
example: Bad: "Safe outputs". Good: < 0.1% of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by the content filter.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

definition: Most use cases need evaluation along several success criteria at once, such as task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy, latency and price.
whyItMatters: One accuracy number isn't enough: the guide's good example pairs an F1 target with toxicity and response-time targets.
example: On 10,000 held-out posts: F1 ≥ 0.85, 99.5% of outputs non-toxic, 95% response time < 200ms.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

definition: Signs an LLM like Claude fits a classification task better: little labeled data, changing categories, unstructured text, semantic rules, need for explanations.
whyItMatters: Claude can classify with a few dozen labeled examples and adapt to new classes without extensive relabeling; traditional ML needs massive labeled datasets.
example: Also: edge cases and ambiguous inputs; many languages without separate models.

definition: Two ways to pick a starting model: fast and cheap (Claude Haiku 4.5), upgrading only if needed, or strongest (Claude Opus 5.5), optimizing down.
whyItMatters: Efficiency-first suits tight latency, cost-sensitive, high-volume straightforward tasks; capability-first suits complex reasoning where accuracy outweighs cost.
example: Either way, evaluate whether performance meets your requirements.

definition: Clear targets that eval results are judged against, such as 95% accuracy, set so you can tell what counts as a good result.
whyItMatters: Raw accuracy and cost numbers alone don't decide anything; thresholds let you tell at scale, with impartial empiricism, which method is best and what to change.
example: Accuracy: 95% (out of 100 tests); cost per classification: 50% lower on average than the current method.

definition: Each Claude model ID is a pinned version: the model stays constant for that ID's lifetime. From the 4.6 generation on, IDs are dateless, e.g. `claude-sonnet-5`.
whyItMatters: A dateless ID is **not** an evergreen pointer. Anthropic doesn't update an existing ID's weights; an updated version ships under a new ID.
example: `claude-opus-4-7` (dateless, 4.6+) vs `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` (dated, before 4.6).

definition: On the Claude API, a short name for a pre-4.6 model, such as `claude-sonnet-4-5`, that points to the most recent dated snapshot for that minor version.
whyItMatters: The pinning guarantee covers model IDs, not these convenience aliases. A 4.6+ ID like `claude-sonnet-4-6` is not an alias; it is the snapshot.
example: Alias `claude-sonnet-4-5` vs dated IDs like `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`.

definition: **Active** (fully supported), **Legacy** (no more updates), **Deprecated** (still works; has a replacement and retirement date), **Retired** (requests fail).
whyItMatters: Deprecated models are likely less reliable. Publicly released models get at least 60 days' notice; migrate all usage before the retirement date.
example: Find stragglers: Console Usage page → Export → CSV of usage by API key and model.

definition: Anthropic's flow for building an LLM feature: test cases, preliminary prompt, iterative testing and refinement, final validation, then ship.
whyItMatters: It starts from success criteria and test cases, not the prompt. A/B testing compares performance against a baseline model or an earlier version.
example: Edge cases to include: irrelevant or nonexistent input, overly long input, ambiguous cases.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

definition: The environment variable the Claude client SDKs read your API key from automatically, so code can create a client without passing a key.
whyItMatters: Set it and `Anthropic()` needs no key argument. Store keys in a secrets manager, rotate them periodically, and disable any key you suspect has leaked.
example: `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-...` then `client = Anthropic()`.

definition: Four scopes: **user** (you, all projects), **shared project** (committed, whole team), **project local** (you, one project), **managed** (your organization).
whyItMatters: Pick the file by who a setting should affect: team permissions and hooks in `.claude/settings.json`, personal overrides in `.claude/settings.local.json`.
example: User file: `~/.claude/settings.json` (theme, default model, your own permission rules).

definition: Highest first: managed, command line, project local, shared project, user. A key set at a higher level overrides the same key lower down.
whyItMatters: List keys like `permissions.allow` merge across files instead, and nothing you set overrides managed values, apart from a few security-sensitive exceptions.
example: Team file sets `"model": "claude-sonnet-5"`; your `.claude/settings.local.json` can pick Opus for you alone.

definition: **Local** (the default; this project, private), **project** (`.mcp.json`, shared via version control) and **user** (all your projects, private).
whyItMatters: Local and user servers are stored in `~/.claude.json`, not the repo. A name defined in several scopes uses local, then project, then user; fields aren't merged.
example: `claude mcp add --transport http shared-server --scope project https://example.com/mcp`

source.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

definition: The file at the project root that holds project-scoped MCP servers. Check it into version control so everyone on the team gets the same MCP tools.
whyItMatters: It expands `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}`, but in a remote server's `url` and `headers` credential names like `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` read as empty.
example: `"Authorization": "Bearer ${API_KEY}"` in a server's `headers`.

source.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

definition: An optional file at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` carrying a plugin's metadata; `name` is the only required key.
whyItMatters: Only the manifest goes in `.claude-plugin/`. Every other file sits at the plugin root, where the defaults are `skills/`, `hooks/hooks.json` and `.mcp.json`.
example: A plugin's MCP servers go in `.mcp.json` at the plugin root, or in the manifest's `mcpServers` key.

definition: The Messages API keeps no conversation state between calls: you always send the full conversational history with each request.
whyItMatters: A chatbot that sends only the newest message loses context. Build the conversation up over time by resending every turn in `messages`.
example: Earlier turns don't have to come from Claude: you can include synthetic `assistant` messages.

definition: Claude is trained on alternating `user` and `assistant` turns. Consecutive turns with the same role in a request are combined into a single turn.
whyItMatters: Two `user` messages in a row are merged into one turn rather than answered separately, so model the history as alternating turns.
example: A three-turn history: `user` → `assistant` → `user`. Claude then generates the next `assistant` turn.

definition: An input message's `content` is a string or an array of typed blocks. A string is shorthand for one block of type `text`.
whyItMatters: Anything beyond plain text, such as an `image` block, uses the array form. Responses also return `content` as an array of blocks.
example: `{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Hello, Claude"}]}`

definition: A Messages API response: role assistant, `content` as an array of typed blocks, and fields such as `stop_reason`, usage, id and model.
whyItMatters: Don't assume the first block is text: each block has a `type` (text, tool_use, thinking and others) that determines its shape.
example: Simplest reply: `"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Hi, I'm Claude."}]`

definition: An `image` content block's source can be base64 data, a URL to a hosted image, or a `file_id` from the Files API.
whyItMatters: For an image you use repeatedly, upload it once and reference the `file_id` instead of resending base64. Claude works best with images before text.
example: Supported formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP. On Bedrock and Google Cloud, only base64 is currently available.

definition: If one API request contains more than 20 images, a stricter per-image dimension limit applies to every image in that request.
whyItMatters: Resent images from earlier turns count too. Stay under it by resizing each image to at most 2000 px per side, or sending 20 or fewer.
example: API maximums: 100 images per request on 200k-context models, 600 on others; 8000x8000 px per image.

definition: A Messages API parameter: custom text sequences that make the model stop generating when it encounters one of them.
whyItMatters: When one matches, `stop_reason` is `"stop_sequence"` and the response's `stop_sequence` field holds the matched string.
example: `"stop_sequences": ["</answer>"]` stops generation when Claude emits the closing tag.

definition: Within an API version, Anthropic preserves existing input and output parameters, but may add optional inputs and new output values.
whyItMatters: New enum variants, such as streaming event types, can appear without a version change, so don't write clients that break on additions.
example: Latest listed version: `2023-06-01`. Earlier versions are deprecated and may be unavailable for new users.

definition: Each HTTP error has a type: 400 invalid_request_error, 401 authentication_error, 403 permission_error, 404 not_found_error, 429 rate_limit_error.
whyItMatters: 401: an API key issue. 403: the key lacks permission. 500 `api_error`, 529 `overloaded_error`: Anthropic's side.
example: 413 `request_too_large`: too many bytes. 402 `billing_error`: billing or payment.

definition: The errors page's advice for a 500 `api_error`: retry the request with exponential backoff, and contact support with the request ID if it persists.
whyItMatters: Backoff suits transient failures like 500s. A 400 `invalid_request_error` means an issue with the format or content of your request.
example: The official SDKs already retry 5xx errors with backoff, twice by default; `max_retries` configures that.

definition: The API is temporarily overloaded. 529 errors can occur when the API experiences high traffic across all users.
whyItMatters: It isn't your organization's rate limit (that's 429). In rare cases, a sharp jump in your own usage brings 429 acceleration limits instead, so ramp up gradually.
example: The official SDKs automatically retry 5xx server errors like this, twice by default.

definition: Sent with a 429 rate-limit error: the number of seconds to wait until you can retry the request. Earlier retries will fail.
whyItMatters: Wait at least that long before retrying. A 429 with no `retry-after` may be the monthly spend cap, where retries fail until access resumes.
example: `retry-after: 20` means wait 20 seconds before sending the request again.

definition: A 429 `rate_limit_error` returned once your organization reaches its tier's monthly spend cap. It has no `retry-after` header.
whyItMatters: Retrying, including the SDKs' automatic retries, fails until access resumes. On the Messages API, `error.details.error_code` is `enforced_spend_limit_reached`.
example: Access resumes at 00:00 UTC on the first day of the next month, or sooner by moving to a higher tier.

definition: Response headers showing the limit enforced, what remains and when it fully replenishes, for requests, tokens, input tokens and output tokens.
whyItMatters: Read the `-remaining` and `-reset` values to pace your client before it runs into 429 errors.
example: `anthropic-ratelimit-requests-remaining`; the `-reset` headers give times in RFC 3339 format.

definition: The algorithm the API uses for rate limiting: capacity is continuously replenished up to your maximum, rather than reset at fixed intervals.
whyItMatters: Limits can apply over shorter intervals: 60 requests per minute might be enforced as 1 per second, so short bursts can trigger 429s.
example: Spread 60 requests across the minute instead of sending them all in the first second.

definition: For most Claude models, only uncached input tokens count toward input-tokens-per-minute (ITPM) limits; tokens read from cache don't.
whyItMatters: Caching raises effective throughput: with a 2M ITPM limit and an 80% cache hit rate, you could process about 10M total input tokens a minute.
example: Counted: `input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`. Not counted (most models): `cache_read_input_tokens`.

definition: A unique identifier on every API response, sent in the `request-id` header and in error response bodies as `request_id`.
whyItMatters: Include it when you contact support about a specific request. The Python and TypeScript SDKs expose it as `_request_id` on responses.
example: `print(f"Request ID: {message._request_id}")`

definition: The Python SDK's asynchronous client. It has the same interface as the sync `Anthropic` client, with calls you `await`.
whyItMatters: Use it in asyncio code. For better concurrency, the SDK can also use an `aiohttp` HTTP backend via `DefaultAioHttpClient`.
example: `message = await client.messages.create(...)` inside an `async def` function.

definition: Recovering an interrupted stream: save the content received before the error, then send a continuation request so Claude resumes.
whyItMatters: On Claude 4.6 and later, put the partial response in a **user** message with an instruction to continue; on 4.5 and earlier, it went in an assistant message.
example: Tool use and extended thinking blocks can't be partially recovered; resume from the most recent text block.

definition: Anthropic's post: if a knowledge base is under 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages), you can include all of it in the prompt, with no need for RAG.
whyItMatters: Try the simplest option first; prompt caching makes the full prompt faster and cheaper. The 2024 post says larger bases need a more scalable solution.
example: RAG: chunk the corpus, embed the chunks, then add the most relevant chunks to the prompt at query time.

definition: The decision rule: if someone is waiting on the reply, send a normal Messages request; if immediate responses aren't required, batch the work.
whyItMatters: Batching fits large volumes of data, cost optimization and large-scale evaluations or analyses, trading immediate replies for async processing.
example: Nightly review summaries: batch. A chat reply a user is waiting for: a direct Messages call.

definition: A unique ID you give each request in a Message Batch (1 to 64 letters, digits, hyphens or underscores) to match it with its result.
whyItMatters: Batch results can be returned in any order, so match each result to its request by `custom_id`, never by position.
example: `"custom_id": "review-10432"` lets you write each summary back to the right row.

definition: The time from sending the prompt until the model generates the first token of its response.
whyItMatters: Particularly relevant with streaming, when you want a responsive experience. Baseline latency instead covers processing the prompt and generating the response.

definition: Anthropic's latency guide: choose the right model, minimize prompt and output tokens, and stream responses.
whyItMatters: Engineer a prompt that works well first, then reduce latency: doing it prematurely might hide what top performance looks like.
example: Ask for a sentence or paragraph count rather than a word count. Claude Haiku 4.5 offers the fastest response times.

definition: An API feature that returns the exact document passages supporting each claim. Turn it on with `citations.enabled=true` on each document.
whyItMatters: Unlike prompt-based quoting, citations are guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents. Enable them on all or none of a request's documents.
example: Plain text and PDFs are chunked into sentences; custom content documents let you control citation granularity.

definition: The citation field holding the exact passage Claude cites, returned with its location in the source document.
whyItMatters: It is provided for convenience and doesn't count toward output tokens, or toward input tokens when passed back in later turns.
example: Location types: `char_location` for plain text, `page_location` for PDFs, `content_block_location` for custom content.

definition: The structured outputs mode that constrains Claude's response to a JSON schema you supply, using constrained decoding.
whyItMatters: It addresses malformed JSON and missing fields. Citations can't be combined with it (400), and a refusal or `max_tokens` cutoff may still not match the schema.
example: `"output_config": {"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": {...}}}`

definition: Structured outputs compile your schema into a grammar. The first request with a schema has extra latency; grammars are cached 24 hours from last use.
whyItMatters: Changing the schema structure, or the set of tools used alongside it, invalidates the cache; changing only `name` or `description` fields does not.

definition: Upload a file once, get a `file_id`, and reference that ID in Messages requests instead of re-uploading the content each time.
whyItMatters: PDFs and plain text go in `document` blocks, images in `image` blocks. Convert unsupported types such as .docx or .xlsx to plain text first.
example: Files you upload can't be downloaded; only files created by skills or code execution can.

definition: Uploaded files can't be modified or renamed. They persist until you delete them or they reach an optional `expires_at`, set once at upload.
whyItMatters: To change content, upload a new file and delete the old one. Deleted files can't be recovered, and requests that reference an expired file fail.
example: `expires_in_seconds` at upload: from 3,600 (1 hour) to 7,776,000 (90 days).

definition: Once a batch ends, each request has one result type: succeeded, errored, canceled or expired. Only succeeded results include the message.
whyItMatters: You aren't billed for errored, canceled or expired requests. Check `request_counts` for totals and add your own retry logic for failed requests.
example: `expired`: the batch reached its 24-hour expiration before the request was sent to the model.
